title: Projectors, TouchDesigner, guest speakers and a depth camera
introduction:
Tuesday: four artists, a projector and my first TouchDesigner network. This morning, I introduced four artists to the whole class: two working in virtual reality (VR) and two in projection mapping. Boyd’s feedback was encouraging. When I spoke about sound driving a character, he said these are “exactly the kind of projects we’re looking at”. He also noted my interest in walls of characters and said that “text as texture is a really interesting phenomenon”. These two comments have given me even greater confidence in the direction of my thinking.

Afterwards, we each set up a projector. Although I’ve seen projectors many times before, I’d never set one up myself. I connected an Epson projector via HDMI, extended the screen display, and used the keystone correction function to align the four corners of the image with a folded paper object on the table. Seeing the projected image cast onto a real object was a completely new experience, with a touch of magic about it.
related_work:
Boyd then introduced TouchDesigner. Instead of writing lines of code, you simply connect nodes. I set up a short chain: Movie File In → Transform → Channel Mix → Null. I entered ‘absTime.seconds’ into the ‘rotate’ parameter, and the image began to rotate automatically.

We were unable to complete the final section. I dragged the Kantan Mapper into the network, but the texture did not appear, and during the demonstration, Boyd’s own TouchDesigner crashed. We continued this work during the workshop on Wednesday.
method:
Wednesday: sending pictures between laptops, and my phone as a controller. Today’s workshop focused on how to enable TouchDesigner to communicate with other devices. As eduroam blocks this type of traffic, Boyd connected the whole class to his own router. We carried out two practical exercises.

1. Laptop to laptop. I connected a webcam (Video Device In) to an Edge TOP; this node converts the image into a white outline and then passes it to a Touch Out TOP. This node sends the image out via a network port. At the other end, a Touch In TOP simply needs to know the sender’s IP address and the same port number. In the screenshot, the outline on the right is the one I sent, whilst the blue image on the left is one that a classmate sent to my screen. No cables, no files, just two numbers.

2. Phone to laptop. Next, I installed ZIG SIM on my mobile phone. It sends sensor data from the phone as OSC messages to my laptop, whilst the OSC In CHOP on port 3333 is responsible for receiving this data. The grey panel in the screenshot displays this data: gyroscope, quaternion and gravity data, all of which are changing in real time. I dragged the gravity channel onto the ‘Translate’ parameter of a Transform TOP as a CHOP reference. When I tilted my mobile, the butterfly glided across the screen.

Initially, no data was coming through because my laptop had, unbeknownst to me, switched back to the eduroam network. Both devices must be on the same network.
results_discussion:
Thursday: two guest speakers on VR. This afternoon, Boyd welcomed two guests: Sophia Ppali, a researcher at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), and XR artist Orna.

Sophia spoke candidly about failure. Her first VR relaxation pieces were not a success, as people felt trapped inside the headset. Later, she developed VR software for musicians, allowing them to choose a room and hear themselves playing in it in real time. In another project, she ran twenty workshops with people living with dementia. Participants handcrafted small models of places that held special significance for them, which were subsequently transformed into VR. She explained that the VR was meaningful only because the content came from the participants themselves.

Orna demonstrated how she paints and performs within the worlds she creates. In her stage show, she projects holograms onto gauze and plays every character herself using motion capture. One point she raised during the discussion stayed with me: VR is a tool, not the artwork, just as a paintbrush is not the painting.

This was very helpful for my Project 2. I have to choose between projection and VR for my breaking wall. Both speakers mentioned that headsets can put some people off, so I will complete the projection version first and treat VR as a second way in. The work must stand on its story, rather than relying on the headset.
conclusion_future_work:
Friday: a depth camera. Friday’s session was relatively short. Boyd demonstrated an Orbbec depth camera connected to TouchDesigner. It works in a similar way to the older Xbox Kinect: in addition to the standard colour image, it generates a depth image in which closer objects appear darker; it is also capable of finding the outline of a person and estimating a skeleton, including shoulders, elbows and hands.

He candidly admitted that part of the example network was broken, and we watched as he got the skeleton working again. One remark in particular was very enlightening: detecting a pose can be the same as pressing a button; it is simply a different kind of input. In my Project 2, the input will be a knock picked up by a microphone, so for me, a sound is that ‘button’.

The session concluded with a demonstration of a 3D scanner, which turns a real object into a 3D model. For Project 2, I am now considering scanning a real stone mortar and pestle rather than modelling them by hand in Blender. I will ask Boyd whether a scanned object counts as my own model.
